blocks.text: Two 40 mm shafts, one plain-carbon and one chromium-molybdenum steel, are quenched in oil from the same temperature. When cut open and tested, the plain-carbon shaft is hard only in a thin skin, while the alloy shaft is hard almost to its centre. Hardenability is the property that explains the difference.

blocks.markdown: When a section is quenched, the surface cools faster than the centre. Only where the cooling rate exceeds the critical cooling rate does austenite turn to martensite; deeper inside, it turns into softer pearlite or bainite. **Hardenability** is how deep a steel can be hardened, and it is not the same as the hardness of the martensite itself, which depends mainly on carbon content.

blocks.title: Jominy end-quench test
blocks.text: A standard bar (about 25 mm in diameter and 100 mm long) is austenitised and then quenched with a water jet on one end only. This produces a steady range of cooling rates along its length. Hardness is measured at regular intervals from the quenched end, and plotted against distance to give the hardenability curve.

blocks.markdown: The quenched end cools fastest and is hardest. Hardness falls with distance as the cooling rate falls and pearlite and bainite replace martensite. A *flat* curve, with high hardness far from the end, means high hardenability; a *steep* curve means low hardenability. Because a given distance on the bar corresponds to a particular cooling rate, the curve can be used to compare steels directly.

blocks.caption: Illustrative Jominy data; the maximum hardness is similar because the carbon content is the same.

blocks.title: Comparing hardenability from Jominy data
blocks.prompt: Using the table above, find the depth from the quenched end to which each steel stays at or above 50 HRC, assuming linear interpolation.

steps.text: Steel A: 58 HRC at 1.5 mm and 45 HRC at 6 mm. The hardness falls 13 HRC over 4.5 mm.
A drop of 8 HRC (58 to 50) needs $8/2.89=2.77$ mm beyond 1.5 mm.
Steel B: 51 HRC at 12 mm and 45 HRC at 20 mm. A drop of 1 HRC beyond 12 mm needs $1/0.75=1.33$ mm.

blocks.answer: Steel A stays at or above 50 HRC to about 4.3 mm and Steel B to about 13.3 mm, so B has about three times the hardenability depth.

blocks.markdown: **Alloying elements and hardenability.** Mn, Cr, Mo and Ni dissolved in austenite slow the diffusional transformations to ferrite, pearlite and bainite. On a cooling-transformation diagram this moves the pearlite nose to longer times, so a slower cooling rate still reaches martensite. The critical cooling rate falls and martensite forms deeper into the section, or larger sections can be hardened with a gentler quenchant such as oil, which reduces distortion and cracking. Alloying does not appreciably change the hardness of the martensite, which depends mainly on carbon.

blocks.title: Meeting a specification
blocks.prompt: A shaft must be at least 45 HRC at 15 mm from the quenched end in a Jominy test. Do steels A and B pass?

steps.text: Steel A reads 33 HRC at 12 mm and 28 HRC at 20 mm, so at 15 mm it is below 33 HRC, which is less than 45 HRC.
Steel B: 51 HRC at 12 mm and 45 HRC at 20 mm, falling 0.75 HRC/mm, so at 15 mm:
Compare with the requirement of 45 HRC.

blocks.answer: Steel A fails; Steel B passes with about 48.8 HRC at 15 mm.

blocks.caption: Case-hardening routes for a gear tooth (typical values only).

blocks.markdown: **Surface treatments for a gear tooth.** A gear tooth needs a hard surface to resist wear and contact fatigue but a tough core to resist shock. *Carburising* adds carbon to a low-carbon steel surface, which is then quenched to martensite while the core stays soft and tough. *Nitriding* diffuses nitrogen into the surface at a low temperature to form hard nitrides, with no quench and minimal distortion. *Induction hardening* heats only the surface of a medium-carbon steel with an alternating magnetic field and then quenches it, which is fast and selective.

items: High hardenability means a flat Jominy curve and deeper martensite for the same quench.
The peak hardness at the quenched end depends on carbon content, not alloying.
Carburising and induction hardening depend on a quench; nitriding does not, which is why it distorts least.
A larger section cools more slowly in the middle, so it needs either higher hardenability or a faster quench.

blocks.title: Match the process to the demand
blocks.text: For deep cases and heavy loads choose carburising; for minimal distortion and a thin, very hard case choose nitriding; for localised, fast, repeatable hardening of medium-carbon parts choose induction hardening.

points: Hardenability is the depth to which martensite forms on quenching, read from the hardness curve of a Jominy bar: a flatter curve means higher hardenability.
Alloying elements such as Cr, Mo, Ni and Mn delay pearlite and bainite formation, lowering the critical cooling rate.
Carburising, nitriding and induction hardening give a hard case on a tough core, with different trade-offs in case depth, process temperature and distortion.

questions.stem: What does the hardenability of a steel describe?

options.text: The depth to which a steel can be hardened by forming martensite on quenching
The maximum hardness the steel can reach, regardless of depth
The hardness of the steel before heat treatment
The temperature at which the steel melts

questions.correctOptionText: The depth to which a steel can be hardened by forming martensite on quenching

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hardenability is the ability to form martensite to depth, not the maximum hardness.
distractorRationale.b: Maximum hardness depends mainly on carbon content; hardenability is about how deep that hardness extends.
distractorRationale.c: Hardenability concerns the response to quenching, not the starting hardness.
distractorRationale.d: Melting temperature is a separate property.

questions.explanation: Hardenability is a measure of how easily a steel forms martensite when cooled, and therefore how deep into a section the martensitic structure extends. It is a function of composition and grain size and is distinct from the hardness of martensite itself, which depends mainly on carbon.

questions.stem: Chromium, molybdenum and nickel are added to medium-carbon steels to raise hardenability. What is the main mechanism?

options.text: They delay the transformation of austenite to pearlite and bainite, so a lower cooling rate is enough to form martensite
They increase the maximum hardness of martensite well above that set by carbon
They raise the cooling rate of the quenchant
They turn the steel into a ceramic at the surface

questions.correctOptionText: They delay the transformation of austenite to pearlite and bainite, so a lower cooling rate is enough to form martensite

distractorRationale.a: Correct: they shift the transformation curves to longer times, lowering the critical cooling rate.
distractorRationale.b: The peak hardness of martensite is set mainly by carbon content, not by these alloying elements.
distractorRationale.c: Alloying does not change the quenchant; it changes the steel's response.
distractorRationale.d: They stay in solution or form alloy carbides; the steel remains a metal.

questions.explanation: Alloying elements dissolved in austenite slow the diffusional transformations to ferrite, pearlite and bainite. The pearlite nose of the transformation diagram moves to longer times, so slower cooling still misses it, and martensite forms deeper into the part.

questions.stem: In a Jominy end-quench test, the highest hardness is found at the water-quenched end of the bar and it falls with distance from that end.
questions.explanation: The quenched end cools fastest and forms the most martensite, while positions further away cool more slowly and form pearlite or bainite, which are softer. A steel with high hardenability keeps its hardness further along the bar.

questions.stem: In a Jominy test, a steel has a hardness of 52 HRC at 15 mm from the quenched end and 40 HRC at 25 mm. Assuming hardness varies linearly between these points, find the distance from the quenched end at which the hardness is 45 HRC, in mm.
questions.explanation: Between 15 and 25 mm the hardness falls 12 HRC over 10 mm, or 1.2 HRC/mm. To fall from 52 to 45 HRC needs 7 HRC, so the extra distance is $7/1.2=5.83$ mm and the position is $15+5.83=20.8$ mm. This is a linear interpolation of a smooth curve.

questions.stem: Gas nitriding of a steel gives a case depth of 0.20 mm after 10 h at a fixed temperature. If the case growth is diffusion controlled, so that depth is proportional to the square root of time, calculate the time in hours needed for a 0.40 mm case under the same conditions.
questions.explanation: For diffusion-controlled growth $x\propto\sqrt t$, so $t\propto x^2$. Doubling the case depth from 0.20 to 0.40 mm multiplies the time by $(0.40/0.20)^2=4$, so $t=40$ h.

questions.stem: Jominy data for two steels are: Steel C 56 HRC at 6 mm and 50 HRC at 12 mm; Steel D 46 HRC at 6 mm and 32 HRC at 12 mm. Assuming linear variation, calculate the hardness difference (C minus D) at 9 mm from the quenched end, in HRC.
questions.explanation: At the midpoint (9 mm) linear interpolation gives the average of the end values: C $=(56+50)/2=53$ HRC and D $=(46+32)/2=39$ HRC. The difference is 14 HRC, indicating that C has the higher hardenability.

questions.stem: A transmission gear needs a very hard, wear-resistant tooth surface and a tough core that can take shock loads. Which route is the best match?

options.text: Carburise a low-carbon steel, then quench and temper
Through-harden a 1.0 wt% C steel by quenching without tempering

questions.correctOptionText: Carburise a low-carbon steel, then quench and temper

distractorRationale.a: Correct: carburising raises surface carbon, so after quenching the case is hard martensite, and the low-carbon core stays tough.
distractorRationale.b: This gives a very hard but brittle part throughout, with a poor core toughness.
distractorRationale.c: Annealing produces soft pearlite and ferrite, with no hard wear-resistant surface.
distractorRationale.d: Normalising gives moderate strength but no hard case.

questions.explanation: Case hardening creates a hard, high-carbon surface on a soft, tough low-carbon core. Carburising does this by diffusing carbon into the surface at about 900 to 950 degrees C and then quenching, which makes the case martensitic while the core stays ferritic-pearlitic or low-carbon martensite.

questions.stem: A precision steel component cannot tolerate any significant distortion, and a thin, very hard case is acceptable. Which surface treatment is most suitable?

options.text: Nitriding, because it is done at 500 to 550 degrees C with no quench
Carburising followed by a water quench
Induction hardening with a water spray

questions.correctOptionText: Nitriding, because it is done at 500 to 550 degrees C with no quench

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the low temperature and absence of a quench minimise distortion.
distractorRationale.b: The austenitising and water quench give the largest distortion risk of the three.
distractorRationale.c: This quenches rapidly from above the transformation temperature, giving some distortion.
distractorRationale.d: This causes the most distortion and cracking, and no hard case on a tough core.

questions.explanation: Nitriding diffuses nitrogen into the surface at about 500 to 550 degrees C, below the austenite transformation temperature, and forms hard nitrides without any quench. The absence of a phase transformation and quench gives minimal distortion, but the case is thin.

questions.stem: Describe how a Jominy end-quench test is carried out and how the resulting hardness curve is used to compare the hardenability of two steels. Explain how adding alloying elements changes the curve and why.
markingGuide: Standard bar (about 25 mm diameter, 100 mm long) is austenitised, then quenched at one end with a water jet while the other end cools in air (2 marks)
Hardness is measured along the length at regular intervals from the quenched end (1 mark)
Plot hardness against distance from the quenched end (1 mark)
Steel with higher hardness at a given distance, or a flatter curve, has higher hardenability (1 mark)
Alloying elements (Cr, Mo, Ni, Mn) delay pearlite and bainite formation, so martensite forms at lower cooling rates (2 marks)
The curve is shifted to greater distances and flattened, while the maximum hardness at the quenched end depends mainly on carbon (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The Jominy test gives a cooling-rate gradient along one bar, so the hardness curve shows how deep martensite can form. Alloyed steels give flatter curves because their transformations to pearlite are delayed.

questions.stem: For the teeth of a heavily loaded gear, compare carburising, nitriding and induction hardening in terms of starting steel, process temperature, quench requirement, typical case depth and distortion. Recommend one for a large gear that needs a deep case and justify your choice.
markingGuide: Carburising: low-carbon steel, 900 to 950 degrees C, quench and temper, case about 0.5 to 2 mm, moderate to high distortion (2 marks)
Nitriding: nitriding steel with Al, Cr, Mo, 500 to 550 degrees C, no quench, thin case (about 0.1 to 0.6 mm), minimal distortion (2 marks)
Induction hardening: medium-carbon steel, rapid local heating then spray quench, case typically 1 to several mm, selective, moderate distortion (2 marks)
Recommendation for deep case on a large gear: carburising (or induction hardening for selective tooth hardening) with a reasoned justification (1 mark)
Notes the trade-off between case depth and distortion, and mentions a final temper or finish grinding (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Carburising gives the deepest practical case and the toughest core on a low-carbon steel, and so suits heavy gear loads, at the cost of more distortion. Nitriding minimises distortion but has a thin case, and induction hardening is fast and selective.
